title: Pointer Arithmetic, Pointers with Arrays/Strings/Functions, and Common Mistakes
description: Pointer arithmetic, pointer comparison, pointers to pointers, pointers with functions, and mistakes to avoid.
objectives: Understand the relationship between pointers, arrays, and strings
Use pointers to pointers and pointers as function parameters
Recognize the most common pointer mistakes

content.heading: Pointer Arithmetic, and Pointers with Arrays/Strings
content.body:
Pointer arithmetic is automatically scaled by the pointed-to type's size: for int *p, p + 1 advances by sizeof(int) bytes, not 1 byte, pointing at the next int — this is what makes ptr + i equivalent to indexing arr[i] when ptr points into an array. Pointers can be compared (==, <, >) when they point into the same array (or one-past its end); comparing pointers into unrelated objects is undefined behavior. An array name, used by itself (not combined with &), decays into a pointer to its first element in most expressions — which is exactly why arr[i] and *(arr + i) are equivalent, interchangeable ways to access the same element.

A string literal or char array is naturally accessed through a char* — string-handling functions (strlen, strcpy, etc.) all operate through such pointers, walking forward until they hit the null terminator.

content.heading: Pointer to Pointer, Pointers with Functions, and Common Mistakes
content.body:
A pointer to a pointer, int **pp;, holds the address of another pointer variable — used, for example, when a function needs to modify a caller's pointer itself (not just the data it points to), such as updating a linked list's head pointer from inside an insert function. Pointers are the mechanism behind C's 'pass by reference' effect: a function receiving int *out can write through it to modify the caller's original variable, since the function has that variable's address, not just a copy of its value.

Common pointer mistakes to actively guard against: dereferencing before initialization (wild pointers); using a pointer after the memory it points to has been freed (dangling pointers, covered in Dynamic Memory); returning the address of a local (stack) variable from a function, which becomes invalid the instant the function returns; and double-scaling pointer arithmetic by manually multiplying by sizeof() when the compiler already does that scaling automatically.

content.explanation: arr[1] and *(p + 1) access the identical element, since p decayed from the array and pointer arithmetic already accounts for int's size. increment(&x) demonstrates the pointer-based 'pass by reference' pattern.

keyPoints: Pointer arithmetic (p + 1) is scaled by the pointed-to type's size automatically
arr[i] and *(arr + i) are equivalent, since an array name decays into a pointer to its first element
A pointer to a pointer (T **) lets a function modify the caller's pointer variable itself
Never return the address of a local (stack) variable, and never manually re-multiply a pointer offset by sizeof()
commonMistakes: Manually multiplying a pointer offset by sizeof(), double-scaling an already-scaled pointer arithmetic expression
Returning &localVariable from a function, producing a dangling pointer to a destroyed stack frame
Comparing or subtracting pointers that don't point into the same array
